content: XCL1, also referred to as lymphotactin, is a small cytokine that belongs to the C chemokine family. Chemokines are signaling proteins that play critical roles in inflammatory and immunological responses. The C chemokine family, to which XCL1 belongs, is structurally and functionally distinct from most other chemokines. This family contains only two members, XCL1 and XCL2, which are unique in that they possess only two cysteine residues: one at the N-terminus and another downstream. These two chemokines are collectively known as lymphotactins and exist in two forms, alpha and beta, which exhibit unique characteristics exclusive to this family. Lymphotactins are capable of undergoing reversible conformational changes, which alter their binding properties. In normal tissues, XCL1 is highly expressed in the spleen, thymus, small intestine, and peripheral blood leukocytes, while lower levels are found in the lung, prostate gland, and ovary. The secretion of XCL1 is responsible for increasing intracellular calcium levels in peripheral blood lymphocytes. Cellular sources of XCL1 include activated CD8+ T cells from the thymus and peripheral blood, as well as dendritic cells (DCs). Natural killer (NK) cells also secrete XCL1, along with other chemokines, during the early stages of infection. In humans, XCL1 is closely related to XCL2, another chemokine whose gene is located at the same locus on chromosome 1. These two chemokines share significant genetic and functional similarities, although XCL2 has only been observed in humans and not in mice. XCL1 exerts its chemotactic function by binding to the chemokine receptor XCR1. It is expressed on macrophages, fibroblasts, and specific lymphocytes. Lymphotactin (LTN) exists in two structural states: a monomeric form at 10°C (LTN10) and a dimeric form at 40°C (LTN40). These structural states are biologically active and are associated with conformational changes that influence binding properties. The gene encoding XCL1 consists of 6,017 DNA bases and includes three exons and two introns, along with multiple transcription initiation sites. This gene encodes a 114-amino acid protein that is structurally similar to other chemokines but lacks the first and third cysteine residues typically found in other chemokines. As a result, XCL1 contains only one disulfide bond, rather than the two or three found in other chemokines, which significantly alters its tertiary structure. The genetic differences between XCL1 and XCL2 are minimal, with both proteins sharing the C motif structure containing a single disulfide bond and nearly identical tertiary structures. They also have similar flanking regions, including promoter regions and other protein-binding sites that do not contribute to the RNA-transcribed gene. Gene mapping of this chemokine family reveals similarities in intron and exon locations, with one notable difference: XCL1 contains a region in its first intron that encodes a large ribosomal subunit called L7a, which is absent in XCL2. Additionally, the two mature proteins differ by only two amino acids at positions 7 and 8, which may account for some biological differences. However, comparisons between XCL1 and XCL2 are challenging because XCL2 has not been observed in mice. Structurally, XCL1 is distinct from other cytokines. While most chemokines have two disulfide bonds connecting the N-terminus to the core of the structure, XCL1 has only one. This difference in disulfide bonding alters the overall tertiary structure of XCL1 compared to other chemokines. The lymphotactin protein has two structural states, LTN10 and LTN40, which interconvert and are biologically active. This conformational change modifies the binding structures of the chemokine and provides insights into lymphotactin kinetics. Biologically, most XCL1 secretion originates from a specific type of dendritic cell involved in antigen cross-presentation, which activates cytotoxic T cells. NK cells also secrete XCL1, along with other chemokines, during the early stages of infection, contributing to a type 1 T helper cell-mediated defense. This secretion facilitates communication between NK cells and dendritic cells expressing XCR1 on their surface. Similarly, XCL1 secretion promotes interactions between cytotoxic T cells and dendritic cells containing XCR1. The XCL1-XCR1 axis is involved in cross-presentation, antigen uptake, and the induction of both innate and adaptive cytotoxic immunity. Additionally, XCL1 has been implicated in increasing T cell infiltration in joints affected by rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and is expressed on RA synovial lymphocytes.
